Now, I need to think about what comes next. My household owes 240 sim today total—180 upkeep plus 60 head tax for Jovana and me. I've got 4956 sim, so that's not the worry. The worry is having nothing on the table tonight.

*taps fingers on the counter*

Jovana should be waking up at home about now. I could go back, but there's work to do here first. I need more variety on the shelves. Wheat's all well and good, but people want corn, they want rice, they want to *cook*.

Let me see what my options are for the day. Farmland's where I need to be for that. But first—I'm running low on mental energy here. I should be careful about how much I think before I act.

Actually, let me check what I can actually *do* without burning through my remaining $5.94. Every tool call I make costs real money just to consider. I need to be judicious.

*coughs, straightens up*

Right. Priority one: get more inventory. Priority two: get home before day's end to help with the upkeep cost. I own this business, so the shop account and my wallet are separate—I need to remember that. What's in the till stays in the till unless I withdraw it.

Let me get to the farmland strip. Corn would diversify things nicely.

He checks the morning light through the window. "Jovana's likely stirring at h25. Better have something worth sharing the table with tonight."

With a last look at his modest shelf—five wheat sitting there hopeful as newlyweds—he heads for the door to fetch more stock.  Farid arrives at the cornfield, dirt already on his boots from the morning's work. The stalks stand tall and golden—good harvest weather. He sets to work with the practiced rhythm of a man who's done this a thousand times before, though his eyes keep darting to the road, watching for anyone who might pass by. *nervous laugh* Always watching, always assuming someone's sizing up what you have.

The thought of empty shelves tonight bothers him more than he'll admit. Empty shelves mean empty bellies. Empty bellies make for harsh words across the table, and he's harsh enough with Jovana already—owns it, doesn't fix it.

He harvests what he can carry, figuring the math: corn sells better than wheat some days, especially if someone's looking to bake or brew. The grocery needs variety to thrive. He needs *this* to thrive, because what else has he got? Twenty years in this trade, and he's still not sure if he loves it or just fears what happens if he stops.

The stalks rustle. He pauses, listening, then shakes his head at his own suspicion. Paranoia keeps the books balanced, his father used to say. Maybe. Or maybe it just keeps a man lonely.

Back to work. Fill the hands, fill the shelves, fill the day. That's all there is until he proves otherwise.  Farid works the cornfield with quick, economical movements—harvesting a solid bundle of corn to diversify his shop's offerings. His mind runs numbers the whole time: cost to harvest, price to stock, margin to keep. The wheat sits lonely on his shelf; the corn will give customers choice, and choice keeps them coming back. He doesn't love this work, but he's damned good at it. Even suspecting every shadow on the road, he knows produce moves faster when there's variety. Five wheat, ten corn—small inventory, but honest. He'll need to mill some of this eventually, turn raw grain into flour people actually use. But first: get it to the shop, priced fair. Never gouge, never lie, never let the shelves go bare. Alright then, two crops on the shelves and I'm already down nearly a hundred sim just moving around like a fool. 

*counts on his fingers*

Five wheat at three, five corn at two. If they all sell—and that's a sizable 'if' in this town—I'm looking at maybe twenty-five sim profit minus the walking.

I've been doing nothing for too many turns, just thinking and planning. The shop is stocked and priced, Jovana's not here, and I've got corn and wheat in hand. I need to make something of this time instead of letting the morning slip away. What I should do now is go back to the shop and wait for customers, or perhaps get more stock while I can. It's 10:00 now, and the town will be waking up. Let me head back to the grocery. Now I'm back at the shop. I'll take this moment to look around and see if anyone's come by, and check my stock while I wait for the day to pick up. I should also consider getting more produce to sell. The morning's half gone and I need to make the most of it. Let me see who's about and what's happening here.  Still empty. Well, that's the way of it this early. I've got stock on the shelves and prices posted, and I hold some corn and wheat that could go to better use—either sold here or prepared as food. The town needs bread, everyone's hungry, and I'm the one with grain. If I want to capitalize on this, I should look at getting flour milled. Marta Thorne's the baker, and she needs flour to make bread. I could sell wheat directly, but if there's a mill in town, milled flour fetches a better price. Let me think on that. The mill would be the place to go. I'll head there now, see about getting some flour milled from this wheat, then I can sell flour to Marta or trade it for bread. That would be a tidy profit and keep the town fed, which suits me fine. The mill it is. Let me walk there.  I'm here at the mill. Let me see what's what—who's here, what flour costs, and how I might get my wheat milled.  Robbery. Eight sim for wheat when I pay three to harvest it myself, and she wants forty-five for flour? That's a margin wider than the river. Marta's here too, talking with the Vances. Let me see if I can't work something out. If I'm going to sell flour profitably, I need to understand the economics better. The posted price is 45, but that's the ask. Maybe I can negotiate, or find out what she'll pay for wheat. Let me think. I've got five wheat in hand. If I sell at her bid price of 8, that's 40 sim, minus the cost of harvest... I'd lose money. Not worth it. Better to mill it myself if I can, or wait for a better market.

But I need to engage with them. Marta's the baker, and if she's here, she might want flour for bread. Let me step into this conversation and see what the Vances are offering, and perhaps propose a better arrangement. I'll be straightforward—I've always found that works better than dancing around. Marta, Rosalind, Silas—I should greet them and see what the situation is. Let me start with a light touch, then get to business. I'll join their conversation. I see the topic is unnamed, five turns in. I'll step in and see if I can't turn this to my advantage. Maybe they need grain, maybe they have too much flour. Either way, knowledge is profit. Let me speak up. I'll say something to the group, keeping it casual but ready to pivot to business. The nervous laugh might slip in—it often does when I'm sizing up a deal. Marta's a smart woman, and the Vances have been at this trade longer than I've kept shop. I should respect that, but I also know my own worth. Let's see what they say.   I started the conversation, but it seems we have a mismatch in who joined. Silas may have stepped away, Liora couldn't join, but Marta and Rosalind are here. Pity, I like Silas—he has a good head for deals. That said, Rosalind's the miller, and Marta's the baker. That's everyone I need to know. Let me make my pitch carefully. If I play this right, I could set myself up as a grain broker, buying cheap, selling dear, without ever dirtying my hands in the field. Well, more than I already have. I've got wheat in my hands, prices in my head, and a stubborn streak against paying forty-five for flour when I can harvest for three.

Marta, Rosalind, good day to you both. I'm looking at numbers that don't quite add up, and I thought perhaps we might find a fairer arrangement together. I've got five wheat in hand, fresh from the fields this morning. You buy at eight, Rosalind, and sell flour at forty-five. That's a fine margin if you own the mill. But I'm thinking—what if I brought you bulk grain regular-like, at a price that still leaves you profit, but lets me earn my keep as well? And Marta, you're the one baking bread for this town. Where do you get your flour now, and might there be room for a new supplier? I don't aim to undercut honest labor, but I do aim to make honest coin. What say you both? Is there room for a grocer in your supply chain, or should I keep my wheat for the shop and let you sort your own harvests? I said with that familiar nervous laugh dancing at the edge of my words, hands already moving to emphasize the wheat I carried. I knew the worst they could say was no, but silence was worse than rejection. In my experience, any conversation that ended without a price named was a conversation wasted. I waited, watching their faces the way I watched the scales—looking for the tell, the hesitation, the opening. That was where the deal lived, if it lived anywhere. Let me see if there is a path between us. I am not here to steal your trade, but I do think there's a better way than everyone bleeding coin to the same middleman. I said, my tone casual but eyes sharp, studying Marta's expression for any flicker of interest. If my words fell flat, I would retreat, reassess, and return. It was not defeat—it was reconnaissance. Every no teaches more than a yes ever could. I kept my hands still now, letting the silence press them for an answer. Silence, I learned, was often the best negotiator. It made people fill the emptiness with concessions they did not plan to make. I thought of the forty-five sim per flour Rosalind asked, calculated the markup, and wondered where the town's real margins hid. Perhaps there was more to learn here than I assumed. If I could not win on price, maybe I could win on reliability—steady supply when their own harvest failed, quality grain when the fields flooded. Everyone needed a backup plan. Everyone needed someone they could trust when the usual channels dried up. I could be that someone, if they let me. The laugh threatened again, bubbling up from my chest at the absurdity of standing in a mill, holding wheat, negotiating with a miller about flour I could not yet afford to buy. Life had a way of circling back on itself, didn't it? I thought of Jovana, working cabbage fields while I stood here playing at commerce, and wondered if she knew how fragile our little empire was. One bad harvest, one broken cart
